paper_title: SCOPE: Semantic Bounded Credit Optimization for Prompt Engineering in Text-to-image Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables language models to improve text-to-image (T2I) generation by rewriting prompts for a frozen image generator. Existing methods typically apply a single signal derived from the image to individual subword tokens, although objects, counts, attributes, and relations form coherent semantic spans. We propose SCOPE, an objective based on Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that aligns update weighting with this structure. The rewriter jointly generates an enhanced prompt and its semantic partition. SCOPE pools shifts in policy log probabilities within each span to derive a shared coefficient for its token losses while retaining a single advantage for each completion. It requires neither separate span rewards nor additional image renders. Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE achieves average relative gains over vanilla GRPO of 9.48% on GeneVal and 7.62% on T2I-CompBench. Ablation studies show that both semantic boundaries and pooling within spans contribute to these gains, supporting semantic structure as a practical inductive bias for prompt engineering with RL.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Text-to-image (T2I) generation models [6, 8, 15, 16, 34, 36, 40–43, 54, 55, 60] turn language into visual
content, with prompts serving as the primary interface for controlling generation. Small wording changes can
determine whether an image preserves object counts, binds colors correctly, or places objects in the intended
spatial relation. As diffusion and flow generators grow larger, retraining or lightly adapting the visual decoder
is often expensive and risks image quality [1, 5, 7, 11, 12, 20, 26, 29, 30, 38, 39]. Prompt adaptation offers a
cheaper alternative by improving the language interface while keeping the image generator fixed.
sections.content: Prompt optimization with frozen generator can be formulated as reinforcement learning problem. language policy rewrites the input prompt, the T2I model renders an image, and an evaluator assigns scalar reward based on the requested composition. Recent methods [15, 34, 55] exploit this feedback loop to improve T2I alignment while keeping the visual backbone fixed. GRPO converts rewards from grouped rewrites into an advantage for each completion without requiring learned critic [28, 46]. The objective applies this advantage across token positions without accounting for semantic span boundaries. Compositional prompt edits to objects, attributes, counts, spatial relations, and scene context form coherent phrases that can span several subword tokens. Tokenizer boundaries reflect subword segmentation and need not coincide with these semantic units. An object description can combine an identity, count, and an attribute, while relation phrase links multiple objects. Words expressing each edit jointly specify compositional constraint, even across multiple subword units. The image reward evaluates the resulting 1 Figure 1. Comparison of uniform token weighting in GRPO and semantic span weighting in SCOPE. T2I evaluator provides single reward for the image. Standard GRPO derives an advantage for the completion and applies it across token positions. However, compositional prompt edits are naturally organized into semantic phrases whose boundaries need not align with tokenizer positions. SCOPE preserves the same advantage for the completion and derives shared coefficient for each semantic span from shifts in policy log probabilities. This coefficient modulates all token updates within the span. composition holistically, without direct attribution to constituent spans or tokens. This exposes fundamental credit assignment bottleneck: uniform token-level updates fragment coherent compositional edits across arbitrary subword boundaries, yet estimating dense per-span rewards incurs prohibitive rendering overhead. To bridge this gap, we introduce Semantic Bounded Credit Optimization for Prompt Engineering (SCOPE), GRPO-compatible objective that modulates token updates across semantic spans. The rewriter outputs prompt rewrite and its semantic partition, mapped onto rollout tokens. SCOPE pools shifts in token log probabilities between the current and old policies within each span to derive detached coefficient. This coefficient reweights the contribution of the shared advantage to each token loss in the clipped GRPO surrogate. The objective retains loss for each valid token and single advantage for each completion. SCOPE uses the existing rendering and reward pipeline, without separate rewards or advantages for individual spans, additional image renders, or learned critic. Moreover, SCOPE serves as strict generalization of standard GRPO, seamlessly recovering uniform token updates when span modulation is neutralized (β = 0). Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE consistently outperforms vanilla GRPO on GenEval [13] and T2I-CompBench [18]. Ablations favor pooling policy shifts within semantic spans over weighting individual tokens, and semantic boundaries over random boundaries or fixed windows. The token weighting comparison tests the contribution of pooling over semantic units. The random and fixed window controls test the contribution of semantic boundaries beyond grouping neighboring tokens. Together, these comparisons separate semantic structure from generic reweighting. Overall, we make three contributions: We identify semantic credit fragmentation in T2I prompt rewriting with RL. single signal per completion, derived from the image, drives updates to tokenizer positions. Compositional edits form coherent semantic spans whose boundaries need not align with the subword boundaries imposed by the tokenizer. We introduce SCOPE, an objective compatible with GRPO that pools policy log probability shifts within semantic spans to assign shared token weights. It retains one advantage per completion without separate span rewards or advantages, additional image renders, or learned critic. We demonstrate that SCOPE consistently outperforms the vanilla GRPO baseline on GenEval and T2I-CompBench. These gains hold across three frozen T2I backbones: Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev.

sections.title:
2 Related Work
Credit Assignment for Sequence Generation. GRPO [46] optimizes autoregressive policies without a
learned critic and shares an advantage across tokens in each completion. Recent work [9, 22, 25, 35, 37, 44,
48, 51] explores finer credit assignment through eligibility traces, counterfactual evaluation, and estimation
over tree structures. Segment Policy Optimization (SPO) [14] partitions reasoning trajectories into segments
and estimates distinct advantages for individual segments. This gives credit estimates a granularity between
individual tokens and complete trajectories. FIPO [33] uses discounted future policy divergence to reweight
token updates according to subsequent trajectory behavior. Our SCOPE retains a single advantage for each
completion. Its contribution to token updates is modulated by shared within each semantic span, derived by
pooling the policy log-probability shifts between the current and previous policies.
sections.content: Prompt Optimization for T2I Generation. Prompt optimization adapts the textual input to elicit desired outputs from pretrained T2I generator. Prior work [8, 19, 21, 23, 24, 27, 34, 36, 42, 47, 56, 57] explores search and iterative refinement strategies for improving generation quality or consistency between text and images. Learned prompt adaptation trains language models to transform user inputs into prompts that the generator prefers. Promptist [15] combines supervised initialization with RL driven by image rewards. PAG uses GFlowNets to promote effective and diverse prompt adaptation, while RePrompt uses GRPO and signals for image preference, alignment, and composition to train rewriter augmented with reasoning [50, 55, 61]. Our SCOPE addresses the optimization objective within this setting. It incorporates the semantic structure of compositional edits into token weighting while retaining shared advantage for the complete rewrite. Reinforcement Learning for T2I Generation. Reinforcement learning optimizes visual generators by treating image synthesis as sequential decision process. Prior work [2, 49, 52] optimizes diffusion trajectories through policy gradients driven by image rewards or through preference optimization. Flow-GRPO [10, 28, 32, 45] optimizes denoising trajectories of flow models, while Mask-GRPO [31] treats iterative masked generation as policy with multiple steps. B2-DiffuRL [17] addresses sparse reward credit assignment within diffusion trajectories through backward progressive training and sampling over branches. Our SCOPE optimizes the prompt rewriting policy through image feedback while keeping the renderer frozen.

sections.title:
3 Methodology
SCOPE organizes policy updates around semantic spans. Given a prompt x, the autoregressive policy πθ
generates a completion y with the rewrite and its span boundaries. The cleaning operator c(·) extracts the
<answer> field, removes the | separators, and concatenates the span text. A frozen image generator renders
I = fϕ(c(y)), which the evaluator scores against the cleaned prompt. The policy therefore receives feedback
for a complete rewrite, although the compositional edits within it can span several tokens.
sections.content: Figure 2 shows how SCOPE incorporates semantic spans into GRPO [46]. Grouped rollouts provide completion advantage, while token likelihood changes determine its contribution within each semantic span. SCOPE pools these changes over aligned spans and normalizes them into shared coefficients. The detached coefficients reweight token losses in the clipped surrogate, with gradients flowing through the policy ratios.

3.3 Semantic Span Credit Modulation
The rewrite instruction asks the policy to preserve the request and clarify subjects, counts, colors, attributes,
and spatial relations. It generates the rewrite and its boundaries in one completion, placing | only between
adjacent nonempty spans. Tokenizer character offsets link the extracted spans to the positions in the loss.

sections.title:
4.1 Experimental Setup
Benchmarks. We evaluate compositional prompt adherence on GenEval [13] and T2I-CompBench [18].
GenEval tests object presence, counting, color, position, and attribute binding. T2I-CompBench covers
attribute binding, object relationships, and complex composition. GenEval training uses 10,000 of the 50,000
prompts organized by Flow-GRPO [28], while T2I-CompBench uses the 4200 prompts in its official training
split. Both native benchmark evaluation sets are disjoint from the training data.
sections.content: Baselines. GRPO with uniform token weights is our primary baseline and shares SCOPEs reward pipeline and training setup. Other baselines render original prompts directly or use the Z-Image rewriter [4] without further training. We reproduce the published RePrompt [55] training and evaluation recipe on Qwen-Image with the same reward clients, rendering seeds, and benchmark harness as our runs. For SD3 and FLUX.1-dev, we use the published RePrompt scores. Appendix A.10 documents the reproduction and score sources. Implementation details. We train Qwen3-8B [59] as the prompt rewriter with frozen Qwen-Image [53], SD3 [11], and FLUX.1-dev [3] generators. We use learning rate of 106, KL coefficient of 0.01, and maximum completion length of 512 tokens. Each group contains = 8 prompt members, including the original prompt and sampled rewrites. All members share one rendering seed to control variation from image generation within the group. Appendix A.2 includes optimization configuration and span weight normalization. Evaluation protocol. Each backbone uses fixed resolution, denoising steps, and classifier-free guidance during training and evaluation (Appendix A.3). We average scores from four images per GenEval prompt and ten per T2I-CompBench prompt with distinct randomly selected seeds. Only training groups share seeds. 6 Table 2. SCOPE exceeds GRPO in every T2I-CompBench category on all three backbones. RePrompt is our Qwen-Image reproduction. Other RePrompt scores follow Wu et al. [55]. Bold marks the best per metric and backbone.

4.2 Quantitative Analysis
GenEval. SCOPE achieves the highest overall GenEval score across all three frozen backbones (Table 1),
boosting overall performance over vanilla GRPO from 0.91 to 0.95 on Qwen-Image (+4.4% relative), 0.74
to 0.84 on SD3 (+13.5% relative), and 0.76 to 0.84 on FLUX.1-dev (+10.5% relative). Across the three
backbones, SCOPE achieves strict improvements over GRPO in 17 out of 18 category benchmarks while
maintaining near-saturated color accuracy on Qwen-Image (0.93), trading a marginal 0.01 fluctuation for
substantial gains in complex spatial positioning (+0.08) and attribute binding (+0.08). Moreover, the most
pronounced improvements appear in object counting and spatial positioning, two persistent bottlenecks for
frozen T2I generators. On SD3, SCOPE substantially outperforms GRPO in both Counting (0.58 → 0.79,
+36.2%) and Position (0.57 → 0.83, +45.6%). On FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE lifts Counting by +0.11 and raises
Position accuracy from the unadapted baseline of 0.16 and GRPO’s 0.62 to 0.84, representing a more than
5× gain over the base generator. These improvements also extend to multi-object synthesis and attribute
binding, achieving 0.99 two-object accuracy and 0.88 attribute binding accuracy on Qwen-Image.
sections.content: T2I-CompBench. SCOPE exceeds GRPO in all six reported categories on each frozen backbone  (Table 2)  . Average scores improve by 6.7%, 8.0%, and 8.2% on Qwen-Image, SD3, and FLUX.1-dev, respectively. The gains cover appearance attributes, spatial relations, numeracy, and complex composition. Notably, on strong backbones like Qwen-Image, uniform token-level RL (e.g., GRPO and RePrompt) suffers from compositional degradation, falling below the unadapted baseline in overall T2I-CompBench score (0.6247 and 0.6246 vs. 0.6280) as well as Texture, Numeracy, and Complex composition, as uniform token updates inadvertently distort fine-grained descriptive phrases during exploration. SCOPE completely resolves this negative transfer, reaching 0.6665 overall and surpassing both the unadapted baseline and GRPO across all individual categories. Beyond achieving the highest color, shape, and texture scores on SD3 and FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE substantially improves spatial relations and numeracy over GRPO on both backbones (+0.0815 and +0.0686 on SD3; +0.0491 and +0.0658 on FLUX.1-dev). In Complex composition, it lifts Qwen-Image from 0.3921 to 0.4473 with consistent gains on SD3 and FLUX.1-dev, demonstrating robust, precise, and fine-grained control over both individual attributes and multi-constraint prompts.

sections.title:
4.3 Ablation and Mechanistic Analysis
Effect of credit weighting. Figure 3(a) compares SCOPE’s span-pooled weighting against uniform
GRPO and unpooled token-level likelihood shifts. Crucially, applying likelihood shifts at individual tokens
degrades performance below standard GRPO across all backbones. This confirms our core hypothesis:
sections.content: 7 Figure 3. Ablation and mechanistic diagnostics. (a) GenEval averages across backbones: SCOPE consistently outperforms uniform GRPO, whereas unpooled token-level shifts degrade performance. (b) Semantic boundaries substantially outperform random partitions and fixed 3-token windows on Qwen-Image. (c) SCOPE remains robust across advantage formulations on FLUX.1-dev, with all variants surpassing vanilla GRPO (0.760) and the hybrid rule achieving the peak score. (d) Training reward dynamics on Qwen-Image: SCOPE breaks through GRPOs early saturation plateau to achieve higher asymptotic reward. unpooled token-level modulation injects high-variance subword noise that disrupts coherent multi-token phrases, whereas pooling shifts within semantic spans stabilizes credit allocation. Furthermore, Token local shift control, which retains semantic boundaries while applying uniform GRPO updates, yields only 0.90, 0.75, and 0.76 across backbones compared to 0.95, 0.84, and 0.84 for SCOPE. Thus, explicit credit modulation across spans (as opposed to merely structured formatting) drives the performance gain. Effect of span boundaries. In Figure 3(b), replacing semantic partitions with random boundaries (0.86) or fixed 3-token windows (0.87) causes severe 89% drop relative to SCOPE (0.95) on Qwen-Image. Arbitrary groupings sever coherent compositional phrases across window borders, proving that linguistic boundary alignment, rather than generic multi-token smoothing, which is essential for effective credit assignment. Effect of the advantage rule. Figure 3(c) evaluates SCOPE under three completion-level advantage estimators on FLUX.1-dev: pure baseline subtraction (bg, 0.827), standard group normalization (z-norm, 0.832), and our hybrid threshold rule (0.841). First, all three variants substantially outperform uniform GRPO (0.760), confirming that SCOPEs gains stem fundamentally from semantic span modulation. Second, the hybrid rule yields an additional +0.009 boost by anchoring updates to the original prompt when initial quality is low (bg < τ ) and switching to fine-grained group discrimination once generation competence is established. Training dynamics. Figure 3(d) reports the Qwen-Image training metric over the first 300 steps, with curves smoothed by 20-step exponential moving average. The smoothed trajectory of uniform GRPO remains lower and varies only mildly, at approximately 0.830.85. The smoothed trajectory of SCOPE lies above that of GRPO throughout the observed window and falls mainly in the range of approximately 0.860.90, whereas its unsmoothed trace exhibits substantially larger fluctuations. sections.title:
5 Conclusion
We present SCOPE, a semantic-aware credit optimization framework for RL-based prompt engineering with
frozen text-to-image generators. By pooling policy log-probability shifts within coherent semantic spans to
modulate a shared completion advantage, SCOPE resolves subword credit fragmentation while requiring
no separate span rewards, additional image renders, or external parsers. Across Qwen-Image, SD3, and
FLUX.1-dev, SCOPE achieves substantial improvements over vanilla GRPO, delivering average relative gains
of 9.48% on GenEval and 7.62% on T2I-CompBench. Accordingly, SCOPE establishes structure-aligned credit
assignment as a plug-and-play paradigm for unlocking the compositional potential of frozen visual generators.

sections.title: Implementation overview
sections.content: A.1 Distributed policy training optimizes the Qwen3-8B rewriter, while separate reward and rendering workers serve the frozen T2I backbones. Qwen3-8B generates the spans during the rollout, without separate span model or parser service. Weighting by policy shifts within spans follows Eqs. 6 to 9 in the main text. The worker layout and hardware placement do not change the objective or evaluation protocol. A.2 Hyperparameters Table 3. Optimization configuration for prompt rewriting, span weighting, and normalization. Component Value Policy model Image models Span acquisition Training data Grouped samples per prompt 8 Learning rate KL coefficient βKL Max completion length Span shift bg,i,s Span raw weight vg,i,s Span normalization Qwen3-8B Qwen-Image, SD3, FLUX.1-dev (frozen, Sec. 4) Qwen3-8B jointly generates nonempty spans separated by 10k selected GenEval + 4.2k T2I-CB prompts 1 106 0.01 512 mean log probability shift over valid span tokens (current minus old) clip(exp(βbg,i,s), 0.8, 1.2) mean weighted by valid token counts = 1, detached Launcher defaults vs. paper. The reported runs use the configuration in Table 3. Local launcher defaults can differ. To reproduce the tables exactly, use this configuration and the same data and sampling protocol. A.3 Rendering configuration Table 4 specifies the rendering configuration for training rewards and benchmark evaluation. Table 4. Fixed rendering configuration for training rewards and benchmark evaluation in our runs. Backbone Resolution Steps CFG scale Qwen-Image FLUX.1-dev Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3) 512512 512512 512512 20 20 28 4.0 3.5 7. A.4 Span Extraction and Fallbacks The rewrite instruction preserves the request and clarifies subjects, counts, colors, attributes, and spatial relations. The rewrite and its boundaries are generated in one completion, with appearing only between adjacent nonempty spans. The separator is not generation stop token. Tokenizer character offsets align each extracted span with its rollout tokens, keeping the partition consistent with the policy loss. valid partition requires valid answer wrapper, nonempty spans, and full coverage of valid answer content tokens with consistent offsets and token counts. SCOPE uses uniform GRPO token weights for malformed wrappers, empty or missing spans, and consecutive or trailing separators. Truncation, incomplete coverage, alignment failures, and token count mismatches also trigger this fallback. We handle one benign end of sequence (EOS) mismatch separately. If the completion mask has exactly one extra trailing placeholder relative to the tokenized prompt text, we retain the aligned prefix. The extra token receives zero weight. The aligned prefix determines the span statistics used to compute the shared coefficients. Table 5 reports fallback counts and rates across benchmarks and frozen image backbones. 13 Table 5. Fallback frequencies in the logged training rollouts by benchmark and frozen image backbone. Exact node counts depend on the notes for each deployment. Table 4 specifies sampling for each backbone without prescribing the cluster configuration. A.7 Environment variables and span weighting Reward services expose endpoints, timeouts, generation count (default 8), and reward and advantage weights. Span weighting reuses the current and old policy log probabilities from the clipped surrogate. Its sensitivity β is distinct from the KL coefficient βKL. A.8 Rewrite instruction The system message asks for exactly <answer>span 1 span 2 span 3</answer>. Before rendering and computation of image rewards, the trainer extracts the answer field, removes every delimiter, and concatenates the span text into one natural language prompt. The format reward still evaluates the structured output. A.9 Reward notes Advantages follow the hybrid rule in Eq. 3. During training, each group contains = 8 prompt members that share one random diffusion seed. This controls renderer noise when comparing rewrites within each group. Groups draw seeds independently, and training and evaluation use fresh seeds across prompts and outer loops. Section 4.1 details the data splits and evaluation protocol. Seed sharing is restricted to training groups. The hybrid rule and shared seeds require no separate reward model or estimation module. A.10 RePrompt: Qwen-Image reproduction Wu et al. [55] do not report Qwen-Image results in their tables. The RePrompt entries for Qwen-Image in Tables 1 and 2 come from our reproduction of their training and evaluation recipe. These runs use the 14 same reward clients, rendering seeds, and benchmark harness as our GRPO and SCOPE runs. For SD3 and FLUX.1-dev, the RePrompt rows reproduce the scores reported by Wu et al.
